blocks.text: Further, by this name the Arabs call the ostrich ظليم [ẓalīm] dtalim, that is, impious, unjust. This name of the ostrich, though less frequent than نعام [naʿām] naam, discussed above, nevertheless occurs in Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, and in Abenbitar, who treat in alphabetical order Of the animals, plants, stones, minerals, etc. that pertain to medicine. And in Damir, besides the chapter On النعام [al-naʿām] the naam, in which he explains the nature of the ostrich more fully, there is also another chapter On الظليم [al-ẓalīm] the dtalim, which begins thus: الظليم ذكر النعام وكنيته ابو البيض وابو ثلاثين وابو الصحاري وجمعه ظلمان [al-ẓalīm dhakar al-naʿām wa-kunyatuhu abū al-bayḍ wa-abū thalāthīn wa-abū al-ṣaḥārī wa-jamʿuhu ẓulmān] Dtalim is the male of the ostrich, whose surnames are: father of eggs, and father of thirty (supply eggs) and father of the deserts. The plural is dtulman. The same word is mentioned by Ibnocholcan, in whom عار الظليم [ʿāra al-ẓalīm] arra dtalim, that is, the male ostrich cried out. It is mentioned also by Nasrius (a writer on the interpretation of dreams, ὀνειροκριτικὸς [oneirokritikos], whom I read in manuscript at Oxford), book 3, ch. 98, sect. 21. And by the Arabic Pandectarius: Talim, that is, the male struzo. It also occurs everywhere in the Lexicon of Alcamus, as these few examples out of many more may show: الظليم الذكر من النعام [al-ẓalīm al-dhakar min al-naʿām] Dtalim, the male, of the ostrich. يرفا الظليم النافر [yarfā al-ẓalīm al-nāfir] Iarpha, that is, the dtalim (or male ostrich) in flight. عمود من الظليم رجلاه [ʿamūd min al-ẓalīm rijlāhu] The columns of the dtalim, that is, its feet. اسقف الاعوج العنق من الظلمان [asqaf al-aʿwaj al-ʿunuq min al-ẓulmān] Ascaph, one with a twisted neck, among the dtulman, or male ostriches. They often fall into this ailment because, when they flee across the sands against the wind, they turn their heads away. الاصنع الظليم متقشر الساق [al-aṣnaʿ al-ẓalīm mutaqashshir al-sāq] Asna, a dtalim (or male ostrich) with skinned legs, namely when it flees headlong through rough places. الحاضب الظليم اغتلم فاخمرت ساقاه [al-ḥāḍib al-ẓalīm ightalama fa-ikhmarrat sāqāhu] Alhadib, a dtalim (or male ostrich), when it is in rut and its legs turn red. This happens to it every year, [col. 234] at the time when the dates begin to redden. جفلت الظليم حركته وطردته [jaffaltu al-ẓalīm ḥarraktuhu wa-ṭaradtuhu] He roused the dtalim, and drove it on, as hunters do. I could [II, 833] bring forward ten times as many of this kind. But I fear I would weary the reader. And these show more than enough that ظليم [ẓalīm] dtalim is the ostrich. Although this name is properly said of the male, it nevertheless seems to be given also to the female by catachresis, καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs]. For thus Alcamus: توحوح الظليم فوق البيض رومها واظهر ولوعها بها [tawaḥwaḥa al-ẓalīm fawqa al-bayḍ rawmuhā wa-aẓhara walūʿahā bihā] The dtalim (or ostrich) thevvachvvacha over the eggs, that is, loved them intensely, and showed how desperately it doted on them. And الزاجل [al-zājil] zagil is for him ما يسيل من دبر الظليم ايام تحضينها بيضها [mā yasīlu min dubr al-ẓalīm ayyām taḥḍīnihā bayḍahā] what flows from the rear of the dtalim while it is brooding its eggs.
